skills.name: Characteristics of protons, neutrons and electrons

note.text:
Particle — relative mass — relative charge — where:
• proton — 1 — +1 — nucleus
• neutron — 1 — 0 — nucleus
• electron — 1/1840 (almost 0) — −1 — shells
Ions: an atom that loses electrons becomes a positive ion (Na → Na⁺); one that gains electrons becomes a negative ion (Cl → Cl⁻).
Electrons in an ion = protons − charge: Na⁺ has 11 − 1 = 10 electrons; Cl⁻ has 17 + 1 = 18.

sections.heading: Comparing the particles
sections.text:
• Proton: relative mass {1}, charge +{1}, in the nucleus.
• Neutron: relative mass {1}, charge {0}, in the nucleus.
• Electron: relative mass about {1} ÷ {1840}, charge −{1}, in the shells.
Because electrons are so light, the mass of an atom is practically the mass of its protons and neutrons.

sections.heading: Ions
sections.text:
Atoms can lose or gain electrons in chemical reactions, but never protons. Then the charges no longer balance and the particle is an ion.
• Lose electrons → more protons than electrons → positive ion. Sodium loses {1}: Na⁺.
• Gain electrons → more electrons than protons → negative ion. Chlorine gains {1}: Cl⁻.
Metals usually form positive ions; non-metals form negative ions.

sections.heading: Counting electrons in an ion
sections.text:
Electrons = protons − charge.
• Na⁺: {11} − {1} = {10} electrons.
• Mg²⁺: {12} − {2} = {10}.
• O²⁻: {8} + {2} = {10}.
Interesting: these ions all have {10} electrons, like the noble gas neon. You will see why in the lessons on bonding.

key_words.meaning: a charged particle formed when an atom loses or gains electrons

mistake.wrong: Na⁺ has {12} electrons because it is positive
mistake.right: Na⁺ has {10} electrons: it lost one
mistake.why: A positive charge means electrons were lost, so there are fewer of them.

worked_example.problem: How many protons and electrons are in a magnesium ion, Mg²⁺ (atomic number {atomicNumber(X)})?
steps: Protons = atomic number = {atomicNumber(X)} (the nucleus does not change).
The ion has lost {q} electrons: {atomicNumber(X)} − {q} = {atomicNumber(X) - q} electrons.

cards.idea: Proton: mass {1}, charge +{1}. Neutron: mass {1}, charge {0}. Electron: mass almost {0}, charge −{1}.
example: The electron is about {1840} times lighter than a proton.

cards.idea: A positive ion has lost electrons; a negative ion has gained them.
The number of protons never changes when an ion forms.

check.prompt: How many protons are in the ion {X.s}? (atomic number {atomicNumber(X.e)})

misconceptions.explain: That is the number of electrons. Protons do not change.

solution: Forming an ion changes only the electrons.

pick.q: What is the relative charge of a neutron?
Which particle has a relative mass of about 1/1840?
e: The nucleus is the heaviest part.
pick.y: Electrons are about 1840 times lighter than protons.

pick.q: What is the relative charge of a proton?
pick.y: Protons carry one positive charge each.

questions.prompt: How many electrons are in the ion {X.s} (atomic number {atomicNumber(X.e)})?

misconceptions.explain: That is the neutral atom. The ion has {X.q > 0 ? 'lost' : 'gained'} {abs(X.q)} electron(s).
{X.q > 0 ? 'A positive ion has fewer electrons than protons.' : 'A negative ion has more electrons than protons.'}

questions.prompt: How many protons are in the ion {X.s}? (atomic number {atomicNumber(X.e)})

misconceptions.explain: That is the number of electrons. Protons do not change.

solution: Forming an ion changes only the electrons.

pick.q: An atom loses two electrons. What is the charge of the ion?
e: Losing negative electrons leaves extra positive charge.
It now has more protons than electrons.

pick.q: An ion has 17 protons and 18 electrons. What is its charge?
e: It has more electrons than protons.

pick.q: An ion has 12 protons and 10 electrons. What is its charge?
e: It has fewer electrons than protons.
Charge is the difference, not the sum.
